what: Acushnet makes golf equipment and apparel. It owns Titleist (balls, clubs and accessories) and FootJoy (golf shoes, gloves and clothing), and Titleist Pro V1 is the best-selling premium golf ball in the world.
customers: Serious amateur and professional golfers, reached through golf course pro shops, specialty golf retailers and sporting goods stores worldwide.
money: Titleist Pro V1 and other balls, consumed and repurchased every season.
Titleist drivers, irons, Vokey wedges and Scotty Cameron putters.
moat: Titleist’s grip on the premium golf ball is one of the most durable brand positions in consumer goods: tour players use it, serious amateurs follow, and the ball is used up and bought again. Ball manufacturing at this quality is also hard to copy.
rivals: Acushnet’s Asian rivals such as Srixon|
risks: Golf boomed during the pandemic; if participation falls back, equipment sales follow.
Net income has barely grown, from $179M in 2021 to $189M in 2025, while revenue rose 19%.
Debt of $855M against $867M of equity is higher than it used to be, partly from buybacks.
Tariffs on equipment made in Asia raise costs.
opportunities: Revenue has risen every year shown, from $2.15B in 2021 to $2.56B in 2025, and to $2.7B over the last twelve months.
The share count fell from 75M to 61M, so each share owns a larger part of the business.
Balls and gloves are repeat purchases, which smooths the cycle.
Golf participation has stayed well above pre-pandemic levels.
watch: Golf ball volumes and pricing, the clearest sign of how many rounds are being played.
view: Acushnet is the kind of business that rarely looks cheap and rarely needs to. Titleist sells the ball that most good golfers play, golfers use balls up, and that gives the company a steady, high-margin core that clubs and clothing sit on top of. Revenue has grown every year since 2021, and the company has used its cash to shrink the share count by almost a fifth.

What has not grown is profit. Net income has been stuck around $180–215 million for five years as costs rose and tariffs bit, so the earnings per share growth has come almost entirely from buybacks. At about 22 times trailing earnings and 24 times forward, the market is paying a quality multiple for a business whose margins are flat.

The investment turns on whether golf’s pandemic boom has settled at a permanently higher level. So far it has, and as long as it does, Acushnet is a steady compounder. I would call it fairly priced: a good business at a full price, best bought on the occasional scare about golf participation rather than today.
bull: Golf stays popular, Titleist keeps its premium and buybacks keep earnings per share growing.
bear: Participation drifts down, tariffs squeeze margins and a full multiple contracts.
